Life from age 4 to 16

I notice how places connect, including which way gets you home if the usual bus does not come. I want to say yes to things sooner, but I still like knowing the backup plan.

  • family: Lives with his mother, aunt, and two cousins after a tornado made their previous rental uninhabitable when he was thirteen.
  • finances: Housing is now stable but crowded; replacement costs consumed savings and adults work variable shifts.
  • geography: Garland, Texas, after several temporary stays around North Texas.
  • cultureLanguages: Vietnamese and English at home; family recipes connect relatives whose memories of the same dish differ.
  • school: Public high school, his third school in four years.
  • accessOpportunities: Dallas College events, a nearby library, and school transportation offer opportunities; fees and late rides still limit participation.
  • Age 4–5

    Caleb liked arranging toy buses into routes and helping his aunt rinse herbs. He was sociable with familiar cousins but needed time before joining games with children he did not know.

  • Age 6–7

    He memorized the walk to a neighborhood market and began drawing maps with every dog and distinctive mailbox marked. His teacher appreciated the detail but asked him to make room for street names too.

  • Age 8–9

    An after-school cooking club taught him to measure instead of guessing. He enjoyed helping others rescue oversalted soup. A recorder unit also caught his attention, although practicing in a busy apartment was difficult.

  • Age 10–11

    He organized a family recipe booklet and discovered that his aunt preferred approximate instructions. They compromised with photographs. At school he liked geography projects but found debates stressful when classmates interrupted one another.

  • Age 12–13

    A tornado damaged their rental, and temporary housing meant changing bus routes, bedrooms, and schools. Caleb kept drawing maps because they were useful. Adults handled recovery, while a counselor helped him reconnect with ordinary school routines.

  • Age 14–15

    After settling with his aunt, he joined percussion because the school provided instruments. He enjoyed rehearsals but left a paid weekend workshop to avoid adding family costs. He did not tell the instructor why until much later.

  • Age 16

    Caleb now helps cook twice weekly and plays percussion in school. He is exploring digital mapping through library computers. He likes his new neighborhood, yet keeps belongings packed more neatly than necessary and hesitates to make commitments that depend on staying.

Life now

  • enjoys: Family cooking · Mapping routes · Layered percussion rhythms
  • avoids: Arguments with overlapping voices · Activities with unclear hidden fees
  • activities: School percussion · Household meals · Library mapping tutorials
  • demonstratedSkills: Detailed route descriptions · Adjusting recipes · Coordinating rhythm with a group
  • unfamiliarActivities: Overnight camps · Advanced coding · Organized athletics
  • motivations: Making everyday life easier · Building friendships that last
  • ambitions: Finish a neighborhood sound map · Join a low-cost summer program · He imagines a stable adult home where he can invite friends to eat and keep belongings unpacked.
  • struggles: Assumes opportunities may disappear · Keeps financial worries private
  • supports: Mother and aunt · School counselor · Percussion instructor
  • practicalConstraints: Crowded home · Variable adult shifts · Limited discretionary money

Still uncertain: Will stable housing make longer commitments feel safer? · Is mapping mainly a practical tool or an interest he wants to explore deeply?
